transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Well, I guess what brings me in is... I got pretty worked up in a staff meeting the other day. I just started acting out this whole fall-prevention drill right there in the middle of the room, using the chairs and waving my arms all around to show 'em how it's done. 

Because, you know, falls are serious business. I'm a personal care aide, and I had this one guy a few years back, Mr. Abernathy. Sweet old guy, but he had these awful hardwood floors. Slippery as ice. I used to tell his daughter, 'You gotta get some of those grippy socks on him or he's going down.' She ended up buying him the red ones, which always reminded me of Christmas stockings, and I really can't stand Christmas ever since my truck's transmission blew out on Christmas Eve back in, what, '08? Had to walk three miles in the sleet just to get to a gas station. 

But anyway... yeah, I was doing the drill with the chairs and my arms going everywhere, and I just couldn't seem to stop doing it. Even when folks told me to sit down and take a breather, I just kept going. So they said I needed to come talk to somebody.
Did you hear or see anything during that staff meeting that other people couldn't?

At the meeting? Nah, I didn't see or hear anything out of the ordinary there, just folks staring at me while I was trying to show them the drill. But... you know, sometimes when I'm alone in the hallway on shift, or even just at home by the laundry room, I'll hear my name being called. Or I'll hear a resident yelling for help, clear as day. I always go check, but there isn't anybody there. 

It's really weird, especially at home, because my laundry room is right off the kitchen and my washing machine has this horrible squeak during the spin cycle anyway. It's an old Kenmore. I got it off Craigslist from this guy who smelled exactly like stale Fritos. He told me it just needed a new belt, but I replaced the belt and it still makes that noise. I had to watch a YouTube video to figure out how to take the back panel off, and the guy in the video had this giant pet iguana just sitting on his shoulder the whole time. Just staring right into the camera. I really don't get why people keep reptiles as pets. They don't even love you back, you know? They just want the heat lamp. I had a buddy who bought a snake once, and... wait, what did you ask me again?
Do you hear your name being called or voices when you're not alone, like during the staff meeting?

No, no, not during the meeting. Like I said, it's just when I'm alone. Like if I'm walking down the hallway at work and nobody's around, or if I'm at home, near the laundry room. I'll just hear somebody say my name, or I'll hear one of the residents yelling out for help. Clear as a bell, I swear. I always go looking, thinking somebody fell or something, but the hallway is just empty. 

It's just like that time I thought I heard my dog barking outside, but I don't even own a dog anymore. I used to have a beagle mix named Buster. Best dog ever, but he had this terrible habit of digging under the fence. I must've patched that chain-link a dozen times with chicken wire and zip ties. You ever try cutting chicken wire with regular scissors? It ruins them. My ex-wife was so mad when she found out I used her good fabric scissors for it. She was a seamstress, made all these custom curtains for people. Velvet, silk, you name it. She made this one set of drapes that weighed like fifty pounds, I had to use heavy-duty anchors just to get the rod into the drywall. Drywall anchors are a scam, though, if you ask me. Half the time they just spin in the hole and you end up with a bigger mess than you started with. But yeah, no, at the meeting it was just me and the chairs.
Do you hear your name being called or voices every time you're alone, or does it happen only sometimes?

Well, it's not every single time I'm alone, no. Just sometimes. Like I said, I'll just be by the laundry room or walking down an empty hallway on shift, and I'll hear my name, or a resident yelling for help. Clear as day. But it's not all the time. 

I mean, if it was all the time, I'd probably go crazy, right? Especially at work. Working the night shift is already so quiet, except for the ice machine at the end of the hall. That thing is so loud when it drops a new batch of ice. It sounds like rocks falling on a tin roof. I tried telling maintenance about it, but they never listen. The maintenance guy, Carl, he's always too busy fixing the golf carts they use to drive the bigwigs around the campus. They got these fancy electric ones now, but they used to have gas ones that smelled like a lawnmower. Reminds me of when I used to mow lawns in the summer back in high school. I saved up enough to buy this beat-up old Honda Civic, but the muffler fell off like two weeks after I bought it. Sounded like a tank driving down the street. The neighbors hated me. But yeah, it just happens sometimes.
When you're hearing your name being called or the residents yelling for help, do you feel like you need to do something in response?

Yeah, definitely. I mean, if someone is yelling for help, I have to go see what's going on. So when I'm alone in that hallway on shift, or at home by the laundry room, and I hear my name or a resident calling out clear as day, I always go check. I go looking right away, but... there isn't anybody there. It's just empty. 

But you have to check, you know? It's a safety thing. It's like checking the lint trap on the dryer. You're supposed to do it every single load, but people get lazy. My cousin Danny got lazy with his, and his whole laundry room caught on fire a few years back. Melted the linoleum right to the subfloor. The fire department had to smash his big front bay window just to drag the hose inside. Cost him an absolute fortune to replace that glass. It was one of those custom tinted ones because he lived on a corner lot and didn't want people looking in at him eating dinner. He used to eat dinner on this ugly brown velvet couch right in the living room. The firemen soaked the couch completely with the hoses. Honestly, they did him a favor, that thing was hideous and it always smelled like wet pennies. But yeah, I always go look when I hear them, just in case.
Do you often find it hard to stay on one topic when talking to someone?

Yeah, I guess I do. It's just... my mind goes so fast, you know? It jumps from my job, to church, to my wife, to all these new workshop ideas I have. It goes so fast that I actually lose the very first thought before I can even get the words out right. 

Speaking of workshops, I was thinking about building this new workbench. You need a really solid top for a good workbench, like a thick butcher block. My uncle had this massive butcher block out in his garage. He used to process his own deer meat out there during hunting season. He'd make this spicy deer jerky that would just burn your mouth up, but you couldn't stop eating it. He used this old dehydrator that sounded like a jet engine taking off. My aunt hated that thing because it would vibrate through the wall and rattle the shelves in the kitchen, and it would knock her ceramic frogs out of place. She collected those little green ceramic frogs, had hundreds of them all over the house. Dusting them took her practically all day Sunday. She wouldn't let anybody else touch them because she was afraid we'd chip the paint. But yeah, my thoughts just kind of race around like that and I lose track of what I was trying to say in the first place.
Do you find your mind racing and thoughts jumping around like this when you're relaxed and not in a situation like the staff meeting?

Yeah, even when I'm just sitting on the couch trying to unwind. It's exactly like I was just saying a minute ago—my brain will still just jump from work, to what's happening at church, to my wife, to those workshop ideas. It goes so fast I still lose the first thought before I can even get it out, even if I'm just hanging out talking to my wife in the living room. 

We were sitting there the other night, just trying to watch a movie to relax. It was one of those old Westerns. My dad used to love Westerns. He had this huge collection of VHS tapes down in his basement. Hundreds of them, all lined up on these flimsy particle-board shelves he built himself. One time, the dog bumped into the bottom shelf and the whole thing came crashing down. Tapes went everywhere. The dog—he was this goofy golden retriever named Buster—he got so scared he hid under the kitchen table for three hours. Wouldn't even come out for a piece of cheese. He loved American cheese, the kind individually wrapped in that clear plastic. You'd unwrap a slice and he'd come running from a mile away just hearing the plastic crinkle. He was a good dog, though, lived to be fourteen. But yeah, even when I'm supposed to be completely relaxed, my mind is still doing that jumping around thing.
Do you feel anxious or upset when your mind is racing like that?

No, I wouldn't really say anxious... it's more like... there are these stretches where I just feel so bright and fired up, you know? Like everything is finally lining up perfectly and I've got all the answers. It feels great, honestly. But then, if someone tries to slow me down or they question what I'm doing, I just snap. I snap way harder than I mean to. 

Like the other day at the hardware store, the guy at the register was taking forever to ring up my lumber. He kept scanning this one barcode over and over, and the machine kept making this loud, obnoxious beep. It sounded exactly like the backup alarm on a garbage truck. They come down my street every Tuesday morning at 5:30 AM, right when I'm trying to get my last hour of sleep. The driver always revs the engine right outside my bedroom window. He drives this huge green truck with a dented bumper. I saw him hit a mailbox once, just backed right into it and kept going like nothing happened. The mailbox belonged to Mrs. Gable down the street, she had these beautiful petunias planted all around the base of it. She was out there crying over her crushed flowers for an hour. But yeah, the guy at the store was just being slow and I ended up yelling at him to just type the numbers in, and I felt bad later, but in the moment I just get so irritable when people can't keep up with me.
Do you find that your racing thoughts are getting in the way of your daily activities or relationships?

Yeah, I guess they are. I mean, they put me on leave from the senior center where I work as an aide, which is frustrating. And my wife... she's been having to remind me about chores and appointments because I'm just not keeping up the way I used to. It's like I can't hold onto a thought long enough to finish a task. 

Speaking of chores, I was supposed to fix the leaky faucet in the guest bathroom last week. The drip, drip, drip was driving me crazy. It sounded like a metronome, you know? My old piano teacher, Mrs. Higgins, used to use a metronome. She had this dusty old upright piano that smelled like mothballs and peppermint. She always kept a bowl of those red and white peppermints on top of it. I hated those things, they always stuck to my teeth. One time, I lost a filling chewing on one. The dentist I went to had this huge fish tank in the waiting room with these neon tetras that would just dart around. I could watch them for hours, just zipping back and forth. But yeah, I've also been pulling back from my church friends, and honestly, I'm starting to worry if I can even safely go back to my caregiving work with my head spinning like this.
Have you recently experienced a period where you felt abnormally happy or irritable and had lots of energy?

Yeah, definitely. When I get those stretches where I'm just fired up, the energy is unbelievable. I mean, on those high-energy days, I'll be up cleaning out all the closets, reorganizing everything. I'll rewrite all the care checklists for work, even though I'm on leave, and start planning this massive health fair for the church. I'll be calling people before breakfast because it feels like it all just has to happen right then, you know? 

Breakfast... you know, I used to love going to this little diner downtown for breakfast. It was called Mabel's. They had the best blueberry pancakes. The blueberries were always huge, like the size of marbles. I swallowed a marble once when I was a kid. It was one of those clear ones with the little swirl of color in the middle—a cat's eye, I think they called them. My mom freaked out, rushed me to the emergency room in our old station wagon. That car had the fake wood paneling on the sides. It was peeling off near the back tire. My brother used to pick at it when we were on long road trips. We drove all the way to Mount Rushmore once in that car. Took three days. The air conditioning was broken, so we had to roll the windows down, and the wind was so loud you couldn't even hear the radio. But yeah, I just get so much energy and try to do a million things at once.
When you're feeling really fired up and have lots of energy, do you find that you still need to sleep as much as you usually do?

No, not at all. When I'm fired up like that, I really don't need much sleep. I can sleep maybe two or three hours and wake up way before dawn, just feeling completely ready to go. I don't even think anything is wrong with it, you know? I'll just be up making all these plans while the house is still pitch dark. 

Well, dark except for the streetlight out front. It flickers a lot. It's got this orange glow, like a sodium lamp or something. The city came out to fix it once, but the guy brought the wrong bulb. He was driving this big bucket truck that had a squeaky hydraulic lift. It sounded exactly like the old screen door at my very first apartment. That place was so drafty, the wind would just howl through the window frames in the winter. I tried taping them up with duct tape, but the tape just got all hot in the summer and left this gross gray residue everywhere. It took me three days with a bottle of solvent and a putty knife to get it off when I finally moved out. The landlord was a real stickler about the security deposit, he tried to charge me for a carpet stain that was there before I even moved in. 

But yeah, I just don't feel tired at all. I can run on just a couple hours of sleep and feel totally fine making my plans while everyone else is still in bed.
Have you ever had a period of time where you felt extremely happy or irritable and had lots of energy that lasted for several days or longer?

Yeah, definitely. I get these stretches where I feel really bright and just... fired up, you know? Like everything in my life is finally lining up perfectly and I've got it all figured out. But then, if my wife or someone tries to slow me down or questions what I'm doing, I just snap. I get so irritated, way harder than I mean to. 

It's kind of like how snapping turtles are. We used to catch them down at the creek behind my grandpa's house. You had to be really careful because they'd take a finger right off if you weren't watching. My grandpa had this old aluminum canoe we'd take out. It was dented on one side from when my uncle hit a submerged log during a flood back in '93. That flood washed out the whole main bridge into town. People were taking rowboats to the grocery store. The grocery store was owned by Mr. Henderson, and he always gave out free slices of bologna at the deli counter. I haven't had bologna in years. It always gave me heartburn. 

But yeah, I get really fired up for days at a time, and then I just get so snappy if people get in my way.
Have you ever had a period where your feelings of being fired up and having lots of energy lasted for more than a week?

Yeah, definitely more than a week. I mean, these stretches where I'm just way too energized, barely sleeping, and trying to push all these huge plans through... they've been coming and going for about 11 months now. 

11 months... that's almost a whole year. You know, a year ago, my wife and I were supposed to go on this anniversary trip to the mountains. We had this cabin rented out near a lake. The pictures online showed this beautiful wrap-around porch with rocking chairs. I love rocking chairs. My grandma had this heavy oak rocking chair in her living room. The wood was so polished it felt like glass. She used to sit in it and knit these huge, itchy wool sweaters for all of us grandkids. I got a maroon one with a weird yellow stripe down the middle. I hated wearing it, but she'd always make me put it on for family photos. We'd take the photos in front of this old grandfather clock she had. The clock chimed every hour, and it was so loud it would scare the dog. It was a little beagle mix named Buster. He used to dig holes all over the backyard looking for moles. 

But yeah, it's been about 11 months of those high-energy periods coming and going.
Do you ever feel really down or depressed after one of these high-energy periods is over?

Down? No, I don't think so. I haven't really noticed feeling sad or depressed or anything once the energy finally wears off. I mostly just go back to my regular schedule. I'm a personal care aide, so I'm always on my feet anyway. 

Speaking of feet, I had to buy these special orthopedic shoes last month because my arches were just killing me. They cost like a hundred and twenty bucks. I got them at that shoe store in the strip mall, the one right next to the old Chinese buffet that closed down. Man, that buffet was great. They had these little crab rangoon things that were just loaded with cream cheese. I tried making them at home once, but the oil got way too hot and I completely smoked out the kitchen and set off the alarm. The smoke detector in my place is super sensitive. If you even look at the toaster wrong, it starts blaring. It's one of those hardwired ones too, so you can't just take the battery out when it acts up. You have to stand on a kitchen chair and wave a dish towel at it for like ten minutes just to get it to shut up. My neighbors probably think I'm crazy with all the racket. 

But, uh... what was the question? Oh, feeling depressed. Yeah, no, I don't really get down like that.
Do you ever feel like you crash or come down after one of these high-energy periods are over?

Crash? No, not really. I mean, I don't feel like I crash. The energy kind of just goes back to normal, you know? Like I'm just back to doing what I usually do. 

Which is a lot, honestly, because my schedule is always shifting. Last week they had me on the early shift, and I had to be up by 4:30 in the morning. Getting up that early is brutal, especially when it's still pitch black outside. It reminds me of when I used to deliver newspapers when I was a kid. I had this huge canvas bag that I'd sling over my shoulder, and it would dig into my neck. I delivered the Morning Chronicle, which doesn't even exist anymore. They got bought out by some big media conglomerate back in the early 2000s. The guy who ran the distribution center was this huge guy named Big Al. He always wore these Hawaiian shirts, even in the dead of winter. He had this old Ford pickup truck that he said he bought at an auction for like five hundred bucks. The tailgate was completely rusted out, and he had it held together with bungee cords. I use bungee cords for everything now. I've got a whole jar of them in my garage. 

But yeah, no crash. I just go back to my regular routine.
Have you ever felt sad or empty for a long time after one of these periods of high energy?

Sad or empty? No, I don't really get like that. I mean, once the energy settles down, I just feel like regular me again, you know? Just going about my day. 

I've been trying to get more organized with my days, actually. I bought one of those dry-erase calendars for the fridge. The markers it came with were terrible, though. The black one completely dried out after two days. I had to go to the office supply store to get a new pack. That store always smells like new carpet and printer ink. I love that smell. It reminds me of the library at my old high school. We had this librarian, Mrs. Gable, who was so strict about noise. If you even sneezed too loud, she'd give you this glare over her glasses. She had these glasses with the little chain attached to them so they'd hang around her neck. My aunt wears glasses like that now. She just turned 70 and had this huge party at a bowling alley. I haven't bowled in years. The shoes they make you wear are always so slippery. 

But no, I don't really feel sad or empty or anything like that. Just normal.
Do you feel like your high-energy periods or racing thoughts are causing problems for you at work or in your relationships?

Well, yeah, it's definitely causing some problems. I mean, they actually put me on leave from the senior center where I work. It's been tough because I worry if I can even go back to caregiving safely, you know? Like, if I'm too scattered. 

Speaking of scattered, my wife has been having to remind me about every little thing lately. Chores, appointments... I'm just not keeping up like I used to. She wrote down a whole list on that dry-erase calendar I told you about, but I still forget. She uses the red marker for the really important stuff. Red always makes me think of fire trucks. When I was a kid, I wanted to be a firefighter so bad. We took a field trip to the station in like, fourth grade, and they let us try on the heavy coats and the helmets. Those helmets are surprisingly heavy. My neck hurt for the rest of the day. The guy showing us around had this huge dalmatian named Sparky. You don't see dalmatians much anymore, do you? Mostly just golden retrievers and doodles everywhere. My neighbor has a labradoodle that barks at the mail carrier every single morning at exactly 10:15. You could set a watch by it. 

But, uh, yeah, it's affecting things. I've even pulled back from my friends at church because of it all. Just haven't been going.
Do you ever feel really down after one of these high-energy periods is over?

Down? No, I don't... I don't really get down. Like I said, it just kind of levels out and I'm just me again. 

I actually tried to explain it to my brother the other day. We were on the phone, he called me from his car. He's got this new car with the Bluetooth built right into the dashboard, so he doesn't have to hold his phone anymore. It sounds a little tinny, though, like he's talking to me from inside a soup can. Reminds me of when we were kids and we'd string two cans together with a piece of yarn and try to talk across the yard. We used Campbell's chicken noodle soup cans. I always hated chicken noodle soup, the noodles get way too soggy. I prefer tomato soup, especially with a grilled cheese sandwich. You gotta use the real butter on the bread, though, none of that margarine stuff. My grandma used to make the best grilled cheese. She had this heavy cast-iron skillet that she swore was the secret. She'd inherited it from her mother, so it was probably like a hundred years old. Cast iron is so heavy, you could probably use it for weightlifting. I thought about getting some dumbbells for the garage, maybe get back into shape. 

But yeah, I don't feel down or anything. Just back to my regular self.
Do you feel like you're back to your normal self between these high-energy periods?

Well, I guess... I mean, mostly. There was this one calmer stretch, yeah. I was actually sleeping more normally, which was nice. I wasn't rushing around trying to finish all those projects I started. 

But, see, even then, for like several weeks, I was still hearing my name being called out when no one was there. And I just couldn't shake the feeling—I was convinced the people at work were keeping notes on me. They have these little spiral notebooks they keep in their pockets. You know the ones? They have the wire binding at the top instead of the side. I always liked those better because I'm left-handed, and the side wire always digs into my palm when I write. Being left-handed is so annoying sometimes. The scissors never work right, and when you use a pencil, the side of your hand gets all shiny and gray from the graphite. I tried switching to pens, but the ink just smears everywhere. My grandfather was left-handed too, but they forced him to write with his right hand in school. Can you imagine? They used to tie his left hand behind his back. He ended up having the messiest handwriting you've ever seen. Looked like chicken scratch. We actually kept chickens when I was little. Rhode Island Reds. They lay the brown eggs, not the white ones. The yolks are always so much darker. 

But yeah, even when the energy calmed down, I still had the voices and the feeling about the notes. So, not totally normal, I guess.
Do you feel like you're switching back and forth between these high-energy periods and a more normal state?

Well, I guess if I really look back at it all... yeah, I switch back and forth, but the high-energy spells—the ones where I have all these huge plans and I get so irritable and have a short fuse—they definitely take up way more time than the calmer weeks do. It's like I'm mostly just running on that high gear. 

My uncle used to have this old truck that got stuck in high gear. An old Ford, I think. F-150 maybe? It was painted this really bright, obnoxious yellow. He called it the "Lemon" because it was always breaking down. He bought it off this guy who used to race dirt bikes. Dirt bikes are so loud. There's a track about an hour from here, and you can hear the engines whining from miles away on a Sunday afternoon. I went to a race once when I was a teenager. The smell of the exhaust and the dirt flying everywhere... it gets right in your teeth. You can taste the grit for days. I actually chipped a tooth once, not from dirt, but from biting down on a popcorn kernel at the movies. It was during that movie about the dinosaurs... the one with the Jeep that gets crushed? I had to go to the dentist the next morning, and he used this drill that sounded exactly like a mosquito buzzing right in my ear. I hate mosquitoes. They always bite me more than anyone else. 

But yeah, the high-energy stuff, with the big plans and getting snappy with people, that's definitely been the biggest chunk of time lately. The calm parts are pretty short.

patient.answer:
Well, I guess what brings me in is... I got pretty worked up in a staff meeting the other day. I just started acting out this whole fall-prevention drill right there in the middle of the room, using the chairs and waving my arms all around to show 'em how it's done. 

Because, you know, falls are serious business. I'm a personal care aide, and I had this one guy a few years back, Mr. Abernathy. Sweet old guy, but he had these awful hardwood floors. Slippery as ice. I used to tell his daughter, 'You gotta get some of those grippy socks on him or he's going down.' She ended up buying him the red ones, which always reminded me of Christmas stockings, and I really can't stand Christmas ever since my truck's transmission blew out on Christmas Eve back in, what, '08? Had to walk three miles in the sleet just to get to a gas station. 

But anyway... yeah, I was doing the drill with the chairs and my arms going everywhere, and I just couldn't seem to stop doing it. Even when folks told me to sit down and take a breather, I just kept going. So they said I needed to come talk to somebody.

patient.answer:
At the meeting? Nah, I didn't see or hear anything out of the ordinary there, just folks staring at me while I was trying to show them the drill. But... you know, sometimes when I'm alone in the hallway on shift, or even just at home by the laundry room, I'll hear my name being called. Or I'll hear a resident yelling for help, clear as day. I always go check, but there isn't anybody there. 

It's really weird, especially at home, because my laundry room is right off the kitchen and my washing machine has this horrible squeak during the spin cycle anyway. It's an old Kenmore. I got it off Craigslist from this guy who smelled exactly like stale Fritos. He told me it just needed a new belt, but I replaced the belt and it still makes that noise. I had to watch a YouTube video to figure out how to take the back panel off, and the guy in the video had this giant pet iguana just sitting on his shoulder the whole time. Just staring right into the camera. I really don't get why people keep reptiles as pets. They don't even love you back, you know? They just want the heat lamp. I had a buddy who bought a snake once, and... wait, what did you ask me again?

patient.answer:

Breakfast... you know, I used to love going to this little diner downtown for breakfast. It was called Mabel's. They had the best blueberry pancakes. The blueberries were always huge, like the size of marbles. I swallowed a marble once when I was a kid. It was one of those clear ones with the little swirl of color in the middle—a cat's eye, I think they called them. My mom freaked out, rushed me to the emergency room in our old station wagon. That car had the fake wood paneling on the sides. It was peeling off near the back tire. My brother used to pick at it when we were on long road trips. We drove all the way to Mount Rushmore once in that car. Took three days. The air conditioning was broken, so we had to roll the windows down, and the wind was so loud you couldn't even hear the radio. But yeah, I just get so much energy and try to do a million things at once.

The wood was so polished it felt like glass. She used to sit in it and knit these huge, itchy wool sweaters for all of us grandkids. I got a maroon one with a weird yellow stripe down the middle. I hated wearing it, but she'd always make me put it on for family photos. We'd take the photos in front of this old grandfather clock she had. But yeah, it's been about 11 months of those high-energy periods coming and going.

They had these little crab rangoon things that were just loaded with cream cheese. I tried making them at home once, but the oil got way too hot and I completely smoked out the kitchen and set off the alarm. The smoke detector in my place is super sensitive. If you even look at the toaster wrong, it starts blaring. It's one of those hardwired ones too, so you can't just take the battery out when it acts up. You have to stand on a kitchen chair and wave a dish towel at it for like ten minutes just to get it to shut up. My neighbors probably think I'm crazy with all the racket. 

But, uh... what was the question? Oh, feeling depressed. Yeah, no, I don't really get down like that.

I had this huge canvas bag that I'd sling over my shoulder, and it would dig into my neck. I delivered the Morning Chronicle, which doesn't even exist anymore. They got bought out by some big media conglomerate back in the early 2000s. The guy who ran the distribution center was this huge guy named Big Al. He always wore these Hawaiian shirts, even in the dead of winter. He had this old Ford pickup truck that he said he bought at an auction for like five hundred bucks. Sad or empty? No, I don't really get like that. I mean, once the energy settles down, I just feel like regular me again, you know? Just going about my day.

She had these glasses with the little chain attached to them so they'd hang around her neck. My aunt wears glasses like that now. She just turned 70 and had this huge party at a bowling alley. But no, I don't really feel sad or empty or anything like that. Just normal.

She wrote down a whole list on that dry-erase calendar I told you about, but I still forget. She uses the red marker for the really important stuff. Red always makes me think of fire trucks. When I was a kid, I wanted to be a firefighter so bad. We took a field trip to the station in like, fourth grade, and they let us try on the heavy coats and the helmets. Those helmets are surprisingly heavy. My neck hurt for the rest of the day. The guy showing us around had this huge dalmatian named Sparky. You don't see dalmatians much anymore, do you? Mostly just golden retrievers and doodles everywhere. My neighbor has a labradoodle that barks at the mail carrier every single morning at exactly 10:15. You could set a watch by it.

Down? No, I don't... I don't really get down. Like I said, it just kind of levels out and I'm just me again.

It sounds a little tinny, though, like he's talking to me from inside a soup can. Reminds me of when we were kids and we'd string two cans together with a piece of yarn and try to talk across the yard. We used Campbell's chicken noodle soup cans. I always hated chicken noodle soup, the noodles get way too soggy. I prefer tomato soup, especially with a grilled cheese sandwich. You gotta use the real butter on the bread, though, none of that margarine stuff. My grandma used to make the best grilled cheese. She had this heavy cast-iron skillet that she swore was the secret. She'd inherited it from her mother, so it was probably like a hundred years old. Cast iron is so heavy, you could probably use it for weightlifting. I thought about getting some dumbbells for the garage, maybe get back into shape. 

But yeah, I don't feel down or anything. Just back to my regular self.

Well, I guess... I mean, mostly. There was this one calmer stretch, yeah. I was actually sleeping more normally, which was nice. I wasn't rushing around trying to finish all those projects I started. 

But, see, even then, for like several weeks, I was still hearing my name being called out when no one was there. And I just couldn't shake the feeling—I was convinced the people at work were keeping notes on me. They have these little spiral notebooks they keep in their pockets. You know the ones? They have the wire binding at the top instead of the side. I always liked those better because I'm left-handed, and the side wire always digs into my palm when I write. Being left-handed is so annoying sometimes. The scissors never work right, and when you use a pencil, the side of your hand gets all shiny and gray from the graphite. I tried switching to pens, but the ink just smears everywhere. My grandfather was left-handed too, but they forced him to write with his right hand in school. Can you imagine? They used to tie his left hand behind his back. He ended up having the messiest handwriting you've ever seen. Looked like chicken scratch. We actually kept chickens when I was little. Rhode Island Reds. They lay the brown eggs, not the white ones. The yolks are always so much darker. 

But yeah, even when the energy calmed down, I still had the voices and the feeling about the notes. So, not totally normal, I guess.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's high-energy periods are distinct episodes

Well, I guess if I really look back at it all... yeah, I switch back and forth, but the high-energy spells—the ones where I have all these huge plans and I get so irritable and have a short fuse—they definitely take up way more time than the calmer weeks do. It's like I'm mostly just running on that high gear. 

My uncle used to have this old truck that got stuck in high gear. An old Ford, I think. F-150 maybe? It was painted this really bright, obnoxious yellow. He called it the "Lemon" because it was always breaking down. He bought it off this guy who used to race dirt bikes. Dirt bikes are so loud. There's a track about an hour from here, and you can hear the engines whining from miles away on a Sunday afternoon. I went to a race once when I was a teenager. The smell of the exhaust and the dirt flying everywhere... it gets right in your teeth. You can taste the grit for days. I actually chipped a tooth once, not from dirt, but from biting down on a popcorn kernel at the movies. It was during that movie about the dinosaurs... the one with the Jeep that gets crushed? I had to go to the dentist the next morning, and he used this drill that sounded exactly like a mosquito buzzing right in my ear. I hate mosquitoes. They always bite me more than anyone else. 

But yeah, the high-energy stuff, with the big plans and getting snappy with people, that's definitely been the biggest chunk of time lately. The calm parts are pretty short.
